definition.text: A tradable certificate claiming that greenhouse gas emissions were avoided or that greenhouse gases were removed from the air.

facts.text: One credit stands for one metric ton of carbon dioxide, or the equivalent amount of another greenhouse gas, avoided or removed.
Carbon offsetting means using credits to counter an organisation's own reported greenhouse gas emissions.
Crediting programs let project developers earn credits for emission-cutting projects and sell them to buyers who want to claim an offset.
Carbon credits are one form of carbon pricing, alongside carbon taxes and carbon border adjustments.
Projects include forest protection and tree planting, wind farms, biogas digesters, energy efficiency, carbon capture and capturing methane from landfills.
The underlying economic idea is that cutting emissions costs different amounts in different places, so trading credits can lower the total cost of meeting targets.
Compliance markets make up most of the credit market: about 12 GtCO2e traded, against 300 MtCO2e on voluntary markets in 2021.
Wetland offsetting under the US Clean Water Act in the 1990s set the precedent for carbon offsetting; the Kyoto Protocol created the first international offset markets in 1997.

definition.text: How confident one can be that using a carbon credit leaves the world at least as well off as if the buyer had cut its own emissions.

facts.text: A credit is meant to substitute for reductions the buyer could have made itself.
High-quality credits come from reductions that are additional, robustly measured, not claimed by anyone else and free of serious social or environmental harm.
Quality checks usually cover the baseline, additionality, permanence, double counting and co-benefits.
Reviews have found overestimated sequestration, double-counted credits and projects that added nothing beyond what would have happened anyway.
From around 2020, credit-rating initiatives and labels such as the Core Carbon Principles appeared to help buyers tell good credits from bad.

title: Voluntary carbon market
article: Carbon offsets and credits#Voluntary carbon markets and certification programs

definition.text: A largely unregulated market where companies, people and organisations with no legal duty to cut emissions buy offsets to meet goals they set themselves.

facts.text: Credits are issued under independent standards such as Verra's Verified Carbon Standard, the Gold Standard, the Climate Action Reserve, the American Carbon Registry and Plan Vivo.
Certification programs set accounting rules, project eligibility and monitoring, reporting and verification procedures.
In 2022 prices for common project types ranged from $8 to $30 per tonne of CO2e.
Credits from projects that store carbon, with extra social and environmental benefits, or with recent vintages tend to fetch higher prices.
Oversupply keeps prices low; without the surplus prices could be at least $10/tCO2e higher.
The voluntary market covers less than 1% of the reductions pledged in national climate plans for 2030.
Issuance and retirement of voluntary offsets more than tripled between 2017 and 2021.

definition.text: A usually public database run by a crediting program that tracks who owns each carbon credit and when it is retired.

facts.text: Registries may also hold project status, documents, credits generated, sales and retirements.
A credit's vintage is the year it was issued, usually the year an auditor reviewed the project.
Retiring a credit is the buyer's choice of how to use it, for example to offset emissions.

definition.text: Issuing carbon credits for emission cuts or removals that are only projected, so buyers can claim them before the work has happened.

facts.text: It is generally seen as risky and as producing lower-quality credits.

definition.text: The steps by which an offset project is designed, financed, checked by an independent verifier and registered with a crediting program.

facts.text: Programs keep libraries of approved methodologies for different project types.
Once running, a project is usually verified about once a year to measure its emission reductions.
After verification is approved, credits are issued into the developer's registry account.

title: Carbon offset project types
article: Carbon offsets and credits#Types of offset projects

definition.text: The kinds of projects that generate carbon credits, from land use and methane capture to renewable energy and energy efficiency.

facts.text: Other types include reforestation and switching to carbon-neutral or carbon-negative fuels.
Methane, mostly from landfills, livestock and coal mines, can be captured and burned for energy to earn credits.
Industrial gases such as HFCs and PFCs warm far more than carbon dioxide and are easy to destroy at source.
Renewable energy projects may not qualify as offsets.

title: Land-use and forestry offsets
article: Carbon offsets and credits#Land use, land-use change and forestry

definition.text: Offset projects in land use, land-use change and forestry (LULUCF) that protect or build natural carbon sinks such as forests and soil.

facts.text: Forestry projects protect existing forests, restore forests on once-forested land and plant forests on land that had none.
Soil projects try to keep or raise the carbon stored in soil.
Deforestation, notably in Brazil, Indonesia and parts of Africa, accounts for about 20 percent of greenhouse gas emissions.
Offsets let firms pay directly for forest preservation instead of deforestation.

title: Forestry offset integrity concerns
article: Carbon offsets and credits#Concerns with forestry projects

definition.text: The criticism that forest-based carbon credits often fail to deliver the climate benefits they claim.

facts.text: News stories from 2021 to 2023 criticised nature-based offsets, REDD+ and certifiers.
One estimate held that around 90% of Verified Carbon Standard rainforest credits are likely "phantom credits".
Trees take decades to mature, and no one can guarantee a forest will escape clearing, burning or mismanagement.
Planting fast-growing invasive species can damage native forest and biodiversity.
Tree planting in high latitudes may warm the climate, because dark tree cover absorbs sunlight.
Projects can clash with local and Indigenous communities whose forest use they curtail.

contested_note: Critics and investigative reports dispute whether many forest credits represent real reductions.

title: Criticisms of carbon offsetting
article: Carbon offsets and credits#Limitations and drawbacks

definition.text: The case that offsets let polluters carry on with business as usual instead of cutting emissions at source.

facts.text: Research from the Australia Institute suggested at least 25% of offsets may lack integrity.
A 2016 Öko-Institut study found 85% of the CDM projects it analysed were unlikely to be truly additional or likely overestimated reductions.
Offsets can create perverse incentives to emit more so that cuts are measured from an inflated baseline.
Several standards measure baselines and additionality differently, and no single standard governs the industry.
Companies that buy offsets tend, on evidence, to make more ambitious emission cuts than those that do not.

contested_note: Sources disagree on whether offsets delay real emission cuts or accompany more ambitious ones.

definition.text: A certification label for emission-reduction projects in the Clean Development Mechanism and the voluntary carbon market.

facts.text: It was created in 2003 by WWF and partners to make sure credits are real, verifiable and help sustainable development.
Projects must prove additionality, avoid double certification and contribute to at least three Sustainable Development Goals.
Eligible types are renewable energy, energy efficiency, afforestation and reforestation, and agriculture.
The Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market lists it as CCP-Eligible.

definition.text: A voluntary UN climate framework that pays and supports developing countries to cut emissions from deforestation and forest degradation and to conserve and build up forest carbon.

facts.text: The name stands for reducing emissions from deforestation and forest degradation in developing countries; the plus adds conservation and enhancement of forests.
The underlying idea is to reward reduced deforestation by giving forest carbon a value.
Cutting deforestation and degradation is estimated to be one of the cheapest ways to mitigate climate change.
In 2019 the IPCC put net land-sector emissions at about 13 GtCO2-eq, about 22% of global net human emissions, roughly half from land use change, mainly deforestation.
Countries need a national strategy, a forest reference level, a national forest monitoring system and a system reporting on safeguards.
Because most deforestation drivers lie outside forestry, such as farming, roads and mining, strategies combine forest measures with land-use and agricultural reforms.
Alongside the UN track, many voluntary-market forest projects calling themselves REDD+ issue credits under private standards, mostly the Verified Carbon Standard.
REDD was first proposed in 2005 by Papua New Guinea and Costa Rica for the Coalition for Rainforest Nations.

definition.text: The five kinds of action REDD+ counts: reducing deforestation, reducing forest degradation, conserving forest carbon, managing forests sustainably and enhancing forest carbon stocks.

facts.text: Together they cover avoiding forest loss, avoiding decline in forest condition, keeping existing stocks and managing forests to sustain them.
Enhancement means activities that raise the carbon stored in forests over time, such as replanting or natural regrowth.
Reduced-impact logging can fall under sustainable management of forests.

definition.text: The UN plan for REDD+ to move in stages: readiness, then national policies and measures, then fully measured results-based actions.

facts.text: The first stage, called readiness, covers national strategies, monitoring capacity, reference levels, safeguards and stakeholder participation.
Readiness has been funded through bodies such as the UN-REDD Programme, set up in 2007 by UNDP, UNEP and FAO, and the World Bank's Forest Carbon Partnership Facility.
Norway's International Climate and Forest Initiative, announced in 2007, has funded forest programmes including Brazil's Amazon Fund.

conflicts.text: The UN-REDD Programme was created in 2008 by FAO, UNDP and UNEP.
conflicts.note: The REDD+ page gives 2007 as the founding year (03c0d2bca15d); the Forest degradation page gives 2008.

definition.text: The displacement of forest loss: protecting one area can push deforestation or degradation somewhere else, cancelling the gain.

facts.text: The Cancún safeguards call for action to reduce such displacement, and many standards include leakage accounting.
Quantified outcomes and issued credits are sensitive to how leakage is handled.

title: Effectiveness of REDD+

definition.text: The question of how much REDD+ and other forest-carbon schemes have actually reduced forest loss.

facts.text: A 2024 multi-country evaluation found modest average forest gains, limited welfare effects and impacts not always lasting.
A study of 40 Verified Carbon Standard REDD+ projects in nine countries found less deforestation than in matched comparison areas over the first five years.
An analysis in the Brazilian Amazon concluded that many project baselines assumed more deforestation than comparison methods suggested.
Results depend heavily on the counterfactual baseline chosen, on proving additionality and on measuring degradation and below-ground carbon.
UN-reported results and voluntary-market credits are not directly comparable, since one uses national reference levels and the other project baselines.
Brazil submitted the first quantified REDD+ results to the UNFCCC on 31 December 2014, for the Amazon.

contested_note: Evaluations report mixed, context-dependent results, and some argue project baselines are inflated.

title: Criticisms of REDD+

definition.text: Objections from researchers, Indigenous organisations and civil-society groups to the effectiveness, governance and fairness of REDD+.

facts.text: Unclear land tenure and carbon rights make consent and benefit-sharing harder and open the door to elite capture.
Indigenous groups warn that forest-carbon schemes can restrict customary land use; in 2007 an Indigenous forum opposed REDD outright.
Broad definitions of forest can include plantations, which may reward tree cover regardless of biodiversity.
Outcomes depend on domestic politics, tenure arrangements and administrative capacity.

contested_note: Supporters and critics, including Indigenous organisations, disagree over REDD+'s fairness and effects.

title: Market versus fund-based REDD+ finance

definition.text: The early dispute over whether REDD+ should be paid for by selling forest credits as offsets or through public funds.

facts.text: Critics argued that floods of forest credits could depress carbon prices and weaken incentives to cut emissions at home.
Since COP 17, UN decisions allow REDD+ to be financed by both market and non-market sources.

contested_note: Countries and observers disagreed on offset-based versus fund-based designs.

definition.text: A World Bank facility that helps developing countries prepare for and carry out REDD+.

facts.text: It has a Readiness Fund for preparation and a Carbon Fund that pilots payments for verified forest emission reductions.
Approved in 2007 and operating from 2008, it reached roughly US$650 million after new pledges in January 2013.
Payments are made only after emission reductions are independently validated and verified.
Early reviews found slow readiness grants and less private investment in the Carbon Fund than hoped.

definition.text: A standard, run by the nonprofit Verra, for certifying carbon credits used to offset emissions.

facts.text: By 2024 more than 2,300 projects were registered, issuing over 1.3 billion credits, of which more than 776 million had been retired.
It is the main program for forest credits in the voluntary market and covers almost all REDD+ projects.
It began in 2005 as a quality standard for carbon credits outside the Kyoto Protocol, such as projects in rich countries that the CDM could not credit.
The Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market lists it as CCP-Eligible.

title: Verra rainforest credit investigations

definition.text: Press and research investigations from 2021 onward finding that many Verra-certified forest-protection credits overstated their emission cuts.

facts.text: A 2021 study found that 11 of 12 projects examined showed no difference in emissions from control areas.
A January 2023 investigation found about 94% of Verra rainforest credits did not represent a real tonne of CO2e and that deforestation threats were overstated by 400% on average.
The 2023 investigation drew on one peer-reviewed study and one study not yet published or peer-reviewed.
Verra's chief executive resigned in May 2023 after months of criticism.

contested_note: The findings rest partly on unpublished research, and their reach over the whole standard is disputed.

definition.text: A UN-run offset scheme under the Kyoto Protocol that let rich countries fund emission-cutting projects in developing countries and count the savings toward their own targets.

facts.text: Projects earned Certified Emission Reduction units (CERs), bought by industrialised countries because cuts were cheapest in developing ones.
It aimed both to aid sustainable development in poorer countries and to help rich countries meet their commitments.
From 2001 to 7 September 2012 it issued 1 billion CERs; by June 2013, 57% came from destroying HFC-23 or N2O.
The IPCC projected that using CDM and Joint Implementation would cut OECD Europe's GDP losses to 0.13–0.81%, versus 0.31–1.50% with domestic action only.
Its revenues were the largest source of mitigation finance to developing countries, and a 2% levy funded the Adaptation Fund.
Weak demand after the 2008 financial crisis drove CER prices from 20 USD in 2008 to 5 USD in 2012 and below 1 USD the next year.
Avoided deforestation and forest conservation were excluded in the Kyoto Protocol's first commitment period.

title: Emissions baseline

definition.text: An estimate of the emissions that would have occurred without a project, against which its reductions are measured.

facts.text: Emission reductions equal the emissions without the project minus the project's actual emissions.
Baselines often rest on hypothetical scenarios, emissions from similar activities, or emissions before the project began.
Offsets can create a perverse incentive to inflate the baseline so that larger cuts can be claimed.
In REDD+, choices about reference periods and data can strongly change credited results.
The baseline sets the potential for emission cuts and the cost of policies to achieve them.
A business-as-usual baseline assumes past trends continue with no new policy and often implies high emissions.
An efficient baseline assumes all resources are used efficiently, so cost per unit cut can be high but total cost low.

distinct_from: Global economic costs of climate change

title: HFC-23 destruction credits

definition.text: CDM credits paid for destroying HFC-23, a super-potent by-product of refrigerant making, which became the classic case of a perverse offset incentive.

facts.text: With a warming potential 11,000 times that of CO2, destroying one tonne earned 11,000 credits.
Destruction cost only 0.2–0.5 €/tCO2, while buyers paid around 20 €/tCO2.
By June 2013, 23 HFC-23 projects had received 38% of all CERs.
The EU banned HFC-23 credits from its trading system from 1 May 2013, citing perverse incentives and lack of additionality.

contested_note: Critics condemned the windfall profits, while the Carbon Trust argued that criticising the CDM for finding cheap reductions was perverse.

definition.text: Seven social, environmental and governance safeguards for REDD+ adopted at the 2010 UN climate conference in Cancún.

facts.text: They cover forest governance, the rights and participation of Indigenous peoples and local communities, conservation of natural forests and biodiversity, and risks of reversal and displacement of emissions.
They bar REDD+ actions from being used to convert natural forests and call for protecting forests and their ecosystem services.
They arose from concerns that forest mitigation could harm people through insecure tenure or harm nature by converting natural forest.
Countries must report how safeguards are respected before receiving results-based REDD+ payments.
Because they are broad principles, countries apply them very differently, and how reported information should be checked is debated.

definition.text: A country's system for reporting how the Cancún safeguards are addressed and respected while REDD+ is carried out.

facts.text: It should give transparent, consistent, regularly updated information, be run nationally and build on existing systems.
Countries send periodic summaries of information on all the safeguards, which are needed when seeking results-based payments.
Indonesia's reporting separates safeguards being addressed, with policies in place, from being respected, with evidence they work.

title: Forest degradation

definition.text: A lasting decline in the biological richness of a forest, where the forest remains but is in worse condition.

facts.text: A degraded forest has fewer trees, fewer species or more disease, without losing area.
Degradation lowers a forest's value and can lead on to deforestation.
Unlike visible deforestation, it can proceed without clear signs, making it hard to measure; in 2009 more than 50 definitions were counted.
Causes include over-harvesting of timber and charcoal, roads, mining, urban sprawl, grazing and fragmentation.
One Bolivian mapping study treated 30–70% remaining forest cover as degraded, under 30% as deforested and over 70% as intact.
Measuring degradation remains a weak point of REDD+ monitoring.
A degraded forest has fewer trees, fewer species, or species hit by pests, which lowers its value and may lead to deforestation.
It is one kind of the wider problem of land degradation.

contested_note: The term itself is disputed, with many and often subjective definitions.

definition.text: The systematic collection of data about a forest, such as its trees, timber and wildlife, for assessment or analysis.

facts.text: Measurements include species, diameter at breast height, height, site quality, age and defects.
From these one can calculate trees per acre, basal area, timber volume and value.
It began in late 18th-century Europe from fear that wood, the main fuel, would run out.
Ground inventories are combined with satellite remote sensing in national forest monitoring for REDD+.

definition.text: A sample survey of a forest stand to estimate how much standing timber it holds.

facts.text: Measurements are taken in sample plots, usually laid out at random along survey lines.
Stratified random sampling, grouping by age, soil or slope first, is the most common design.
The number and size of plots set how certain the estimate for the whole stand is.

definition.text: A benchmark of a country's forest emissions or removals, in tonnes of CO2e per year, against which REDD+ results are judged.

facts.text: Results-period emissions and removals are compared with the reference period to measure performance.
Reference levels usually draw on historical data on forest-area change combined with emission estimates.
Each submission for results-based payments undergoes a UN technical assessment, and countries may improve them step by step.
Choices of reference period, data, activities and carbon pools change how many results are counted.
Simple extrapolation of past forest loss could tempt countries to deforest more during the reference period to earn more credits later.
Nesting links project baselines with jurisdiction-wide reference levels to avoid double counting.

definition.text: A country's institutions and techniques for monitoring its forests and producing information for decisions and reporting.

facts.text: REDD+ countries are encouraged to build transparent systems combining satellite remote sensing with ground forest inventories.
Outputs include time series of forest area and change, maps, and biomass or carbon-stock estimates with uncertainty information.
Having one, along with an assessed reference level, is a condition for results-based payments.
Between 2005 and 2020 countries with good remote-sensing forest monitoring rose from 55 to 99, and with good national inventories from 48 to 102.
Sustained funding, coordination across agencies and consistent methods over time remain challenges.

definition.text: A voluntary, non-binding 2014 pledge by governments, companies and civil society to halve deforestation by 2020 and end it by 2030.

facts.text: It also pledges to restore hundreds of millions of acres of degraded land.
Signers included 37 governments, 53 multinational companies, 16 Indigenous groups and 63 NGOs.
A 2019 five-year assessment described large commitments but limited progress.

title: Time value of carbon

definition.text: The idea that cutting a tonne of greenhouse gas now is worth more than cutting the same tonne later, so emissions are discounted over time like money.

facts.text: It is a discount rate on the physical carbon itself, not the money discount rate used to appraise carbon projects.
Pathways that reach zero emissions on the same date emit different totals: early deep cuts emit least, delayed cuts most.
A high carbon discount rate rewards cutting emissions early; a low one weakens the push for immediate action.
If the time value is positive, even temporary storage of carbon in trees or soil has real value because it delays warming.

notes: The page calls it a conjecture; there is no stated scholarly dispute.

title: Over-crediting

definition.text: Issuing more carbon credits than the real emission cuts or removals a project achieved, sometimes producing so-called phantom credits.

facts.text: Perverse incentives can reward over-crediting when buyers focus on headline tonnes rather than real impact.
One estimate held that about 90% of Verified Carbon Standard rainforest credits were likely phantom credits.
Critics note that over-crediting persisted even where programs already applied additionality, conservative measurement and permanence rules, often through inflated baselines.
The risk of over-crediting is a central worry in debates over trading under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

contested_note: Commentators dispute how far over-crediting undermines Article 6 trading and voluntary markets.

sources.title: Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market
Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement

definition.text: An accounting step under the Paris Agreement that subtracts a transferred emission cut from the seller country's tally so that only the buyer counts it.

facts.text: They prevent double claiming, where both the transferring and acquiring country count the same reduction toward their national targets.
Transferred outcomes must be recorded as a gain for one party and a reduction for the other.
Rules adopted at COP26 set out how corresponding adjustments and reporting work in practice.
When a host government authorises voluntary-market credits for Article 6 use, a corresponding adjustment may be required.

sources.title: Cooperative mechanisms under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement
